name: Battle of Madagascar
info: British and Allied forces landed at Diego-Suarez on 5 May 1942 and then took the rest of the Vichy French-held island of Madagascar, to keep Japanese ships from its ports; an armistice came on 6 November.

facts.date: 5 May to 6 November 1942: Operation Ironclad at Diego-Suarez from 5 to 7 May, then Operations Stream, Line and Jane from 10 September, and an armistice on 6 November
facts.place: Madagascar, from Diego-Suarez (now Antsiranana) at the northern tip, in the western Indian Ocean, to Majunga, Tamatave, Tananarive, Tulear and Fianarantsoa
facts.sides: Britain and its Allies, with the landing force of Force 121 under Major-General Robert Sturges and the naval force under Rear-Admiral Edward Syfret; Vichy France under Governor General Armand Léon Annet, with about 8,000 troops, about 6,000 of them Malagasy tirailleurs
facts.outcome: The Allies took Diego-Suarez in three days and the rest of the island by the end of October. Fighting ceased and an armistice was granted on 6 November, and the island was placed under Free French control.

t: The campaign was launched to deny Madagascar's ports to the Imperial Japanese Navy and to protect Allied shipping routes to India, Australia and Southeast Asia.
The Vichy garrison of about 8,000 was made up mostly of Malagasy tirailleurs, and its Joffre line at Antisarane held the first assault until a destroyer landed marines in the town.

It was the first large-scale operation of the Second World War by the Allies combining sea, land and air forces; Julian Jackson observed that the French held out longer in Madagascar in 1942 than against the Germans in France in 1940.
dyk: A Royal Navy destroyer, HMS Anthony, dashed past the harbour defences of Antisarane and put fifty Royal Marines ashore in the Vichy rear, and the town surrendered that evening.
ev: Japanese carrier raids on Ceylon drive the British Eastern Fleet to Kilindini, and Churchill agrees that planning for an invasion of Madagascar should begin
Operation Ironclad: British forces land at Courrier Bay and Ambararata Bay, west of Diego-Suarez
Royal Marines landed from HMS Anthony break the Vichy defence at Antisarane, and Diego-Suarez falls
Japanese midget submarines damage HMS Ramillies and sink the tanker British Loyalty in Diego-Suarez harbour
Operations Stream, Line and Jane: landings at Majunga and Tamatave, and Tananarive falls
King's African Rifles ambush Vichy troops at Andramanalina, and 800 surrender
An armistice is signed at Ambalavao, and Annet surrenders two days later

sections.background:
Diego-Suarez is a large bay with a fine harbour near the northern tip of Madagascar, opening to the east through the narrow Oronjia Pass. France coveted it in the 1880s as a coaling station for steamships, and after the first Franco-Hova War Queen Ranavalona III signed a treaty on 17 December 1885 giving France a protectorate over the bay and the surrounding territory. In 1941 the town, the bay and the channel were well protected by naval shore batteries.

By the end of February 1942 Japan had conquered Southeast Asia east of Burma, and its submarines moved freely through the northern and eastern Indian Ocean. In March Japanese carriers raided shipping in the Bay of Bengal and attacked Colombo and Trincomalee, which drove the British Eastern Fleet to a new base at Kilindini, Mombasa. Japanese Kaidai-type submarines had a range of more than 10,000 miles in some cases, so bases on Madagascar would have affected Allied communications from the Pacific to the South Atlantic. German officers pressed the Japanese to give Madagascar priority, and the Japanese would not disclose their plans for it.

On 27 November 1941 the British Chiefs of Staff discussed the possibility that the Vichy government might cede Madagascar to Japan or let its navy use the island. On 16 December de Gaulle urged Churchill to act. Churchill did not want a joint British and Free French operation after the Battle of Dakar in 1940. By 12 March 1942 he was convinced, the Free French were explicitly excluded, and on 14 March Force 121 was constituted under Major-General Robert Sturges, with Rear-Admiral Edward Syfret in command at sea.
sections.forces:
Force 121 left the Clyde on 23 March, met Syfret's ships at Freetown and assembled at Durban, where the 13th Brigade Group of the 5th Division joined it. Syfret's squadron included the battleship HMS Ramillies, the carriers HMS Illustrious and HMS Indomitable, the cruisers Hermione and Devonshire, eleven destroyers, six minesweepers and six corvettes, over 50 vessels in all. The landing force was the 29th Independent Infantry Brigade Group, No. 5 Commando and two brigades of the 5th Infantry Division. The chiefs of staff were adamant that the operation must succeed, preferably without any fighting. It was the first British amphibious assault since the Dardanelles twenty-seven years before.

The defenders were led by Governor General Armand Léon Annet and numbered about 8,000 troops, about 6,000 of them Malagasy tirailleurs, a large proportion of the rest being Senegalese. Between 1,500 and 3,000 were concentrated around Diego-Suarez. Naval and air defences were relatively light or obsolete: eight coastal batteries, two armed merchant cruisers, two sloops, five submarines, 17 M.S. 406 fighters and ten Potez 63 bombers.

Field-Marshal Smuts urged that Majunga and Tamatave be occupied as well, but Diego-Suarez was kept as the only objective for lack of manpower. Antisarane, the naval base, was elaborately defended with trenches, two redoubts and pillboxes, and flanked by impenetrable swamps. The British were unaware of the strength of these defences, known as the Joffre line.
sections.course:
On 5 May, after reconnaissance flights by the South African Air Force, the 29th Brigade and No. 5 Commando went ashore in landing craft at Courrier Bay and Ambararata Bay, west of Diego-Suarez, while a diversionary attack was staged to the east. Swordfish and Albacore aircraft from the carriers attacked Vichy shipping and Arrachart airfield and sank the armed merchant cruiser Bougainville and the submarine Bévéziers. The landings met virtually no resistance. The 17th Brigade took the town of Diego-Suarez after toiling through mangrove swamp and bush, while the 29th Brigade advanced 21 miles towards Antisarane with a few tanks.

On the morning of 6 May a frontal assault on the Joffre line failed, and by the end of the day 10 of the 12 tanks had been destroyed. The South Lancashires worked round the defences and caused chaos behind them, taking a radio station and a barracks, but withdrew when their radio failed. Admiral Darlan told Annet to defend the honour of the flag and to make the British pay dearly.

The deadlock was broken when the old destroyer HMS Anthony dashed past the harbour defences and landed fifty Royal Marines in the rear, who took the artillery command post, a barracks and the naval depot. The 17th Brigade broke through and Antisarane surrendered that evening, though substantial Vichy forces withdrew to the south. Operation Ironclad ended on 7 May.
sections.aftermath:
In three days the British had 109 men killed and 283 wounded and the French about 700 casualties; the Allies later gave about 500 casualties for the landing at Diego-Suarez. By 7 May twelve Morane fighters and five Potez 63s had been destroyed of 35 Vichy aircraft on the island. On 29 May Japanese submarines arrived, and a midget submarine damaged Ramillies and sank the tanker British Loyalty, later refloated. The crew of the other, Lieutenant Saburo Akieda and Petty Officer Masami Takemoto, were betrayed in the village of Anijabe and killed in a firefight with Royal Marines.

Fighting then fell to a low level. Mayotte was taken on 2 July without loss of life. The campaign to secure the rest of the island opened with landings at Majunga on 10 September and Tamatave on 18 September, and Tananarive fell on 23 September. A landing at Tulear followed on 29 September. The last major action was the ambush at Andramanalina on 18 October, where 800 Vichy troops surrendered. Annet, who had escaped, asked for terms; an armistice was signed at Ambalavao on 6 November and he surrendered two days later. The fighting after 10 September cost the Allies 30 killed and 90 wounded.
sections.sources:
The ships, brigades and squadrons on each side are known by name, and Churchill's guidelines to the planners of Operation Bonus are recorded. The dead and wounded of Ironclad are put at 109 killed and 283 wounded for the British, and about 700 casualties for the French; a figure of about 500 casualties for the Allies in the landing at Diego-Suarez also stands. Darlan's message to Annet is recorded in his own words.

The weight of the campaign is a matter of judgement. Julian Jackson, in his biography of de Gaulle, observed that the French held out longer against the Allies in Madagascar in 1942 than they had against the Germans in France in 1940. John Grehan has claimed that the capture of the island before it could fall into Japanese hands was so crucial that it led to Japan's eventual downfall and defeat. The Japanese refused to disclose their plans for Madagascar to their German partners, and Vichy's request to Japan for help found Japan in no position to give substantial support.
sections.legacy:
With Madagascar in Allied hands, military and naval installations were established across the island. Its deep-water ports were vital for control of the passage to India and the Persian corridor and were now beyond the reach of the Axis. In the makeshift Allied planning of the early years of the war the invasion held a prominent strategic place, and it was the first large-scale Allied operation to combine sea, land and air forces.

The island was placed under Free French control. General Paul Legentilhomme was appointed High Commissioner for Madagascar in December 1942, only to replace British administration. Like many colonies, Madagascar sought independence from the French Empire after the war. In 1947 the island experienced the Malagasy Uprising, a costly revolution that was crushed in 1948, and on 26 June 1960 the Malagasy Republic proclaimed its independence from France, about twelve years later.

Campaign service in Madagascar did not qualify for the Africa Star; it was covered by the 1939–1945 Star.

summary: From 5 May 1942 British and Allied forces took Diego-Suarez and then the rest of Vichy French Madagascar, to keep its ports from the Japanese navy. About 6,000 of the 8,000 defenders were Malagasy tirailleurs, and an armistice was signed on 6 November.
notes: The sources section is thin: the article names few evidence sources. I wrote about what it does give (casualty figures, Darlan's message, Jackson and Grehan). 'Documented by plans and orders' and 'order of battle' are inferences from the article's order of battle section, not stated evidence; the editor may trim.
Casualties: 109 killed and 283 wounded (British), 700 French in three days; 'about 500 casualties in the landing at Diego-Suarez' elsewhere. Both given.
Ironclad is said to have concluded on 7 May, while the article's lead and campaign text call the seizure of Diego-Suarez the start of a campaign lasting to 6 November.
The article says the 29th and 22nd Brigades landed at Majunga on 10 September and also that 29th Brigade fought at Diego-Suarez in May; no conflict.
The Fricke meetings: I wrote only that German officers pressed Madagascar's priority; the article says Fricke stressed Ceylon, the Seychelles and Madagascar over Australia.
The article does not say how Malagasy civilians fared; nothing on them is given beyond the troops and the 1947 uprising.
